strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: continuous-time MARL via HJB-based PINNs, a promising direction beyond single-agent CTRL
The Value Gradient Iteration (VGI) module is an interesting idea — differentiating the one-step DDP to obtain a self-supervised gradient target avoids the need for ground-truth gradients

Evaluation spans multiple environments (continuous-time MPE, multi-agent MuJoCo variants, and a coupled-oscillator toy task with exact LQR ground truth), with ablations on the VGI module, loss-term weights, and activation functions
Provides proofs for lemmas/theorems and an explicit training algorithm, plus hyperparameter and architecture tables supporting reproducibility
The time-discretization robustness experiment (Fig. 8) nicely illustrates the practical motivation for CT methods over DT baselines
weaknesses: Formulation is internally inconsistent: Eq. (2) defines an infinite-horizon value function, yet Lemma 3.1 and the PINN boundary condition use a finite horizon V(x,T)=g(x); the discount/two settings are conflated throughout

Theoretical claims are weak or incorrect. Theorem 3.4's contraction proof (β = e^{−ρΔt}(1+L_fΔt) < 1 only for small Δt) shows the one-step affine map is a contraction, but this does not establish that bootstrapped VGI targets converge to the true value gradient, especially under model errors from the learned dynamics f_ψ and reward r_ϕ. Lemma 3.3's 'proof' assumes a continuous argmax policy improvement and is essentially informal

VGI critically depends on learned dynamics and reward models, but there is no analysis of how model bias propagates into gradient targets or value estimates; the method is effectively model-based while some baselines are model-free, making comparisons confounded

Baselines are limited: only DPI, IPI, and CT-MBRL (ODE); standard strong MARL methods (MAPPO, FACMAC, QMIX-style critics) are absent from the main comparisons — MADDPG appears only in a didactic experiment, so 'consistently outperforms existing baselines' is only demonstrated against a narrow, weak baseline set

Evidence quality is uneven: Fig. 3's gradient contours have color scales (VIP: ~0.095–0.11) inconsistent with ground truth (~0.08–0.093), undercutting the claimed gradient fidelity; some learning curves show large instability; the novelty of combining PINN-HJB critics with TD anchors and policy gradients is incremental relative to [27, 34, 51], and the VGI idea closely resembles classical value-gradient learning literature (e.g., Fairbank & Alonso) that is not discussed

Presentation issues: method is called CT-MARL in abstract/intro but VIP in experiments; duplicate references ([8,9], [24,25]); typos ('chllenges', 'VPI' vs 'VIP' in Fig. 9, 'a reward models'); results reported as means over only 5 seeds without statistical tests; no statement on code release

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem (continuous-time MARL via HJB/PINNs) and the motivation for moving beyond discrete-time MARL is well-articulated, supported by a didactic coupled-oscillator example with an analytical LQR ground truth.

The proposed VIP framework is clearly described end-to-end (HJB residual critic, VGI gradient-consistency loss, anchor TD loss, learned dynamics/reward models), and the appendix includes the training algorithm, environment construction details, and network architectures, which aids reproducibility.

The empirical evaluation covers a reasonable range of tasks (continuous-time variants of MPE and multi-agent MuJoCo, plus a didactic benchmark) with ablations on the VGI module, activation functions, and loss-term weighting, and the value/value-gradient visualizations qualitatively support the claim that VGI improves gradient fidelity.
The time-interval robustness experiment (Fig. 8) directly probes the core claim that continuous-time methods degrade gracefully under varying decision intervals where discrete-time baselines fail.
weaknesses: Formulation inconsistencies undermine the theoretical framing: Eq. (2) defines an infinite-horizon value function V(x), yet Lemma 3.1 and the critic loss use a finite-horizon HJB with ∂tV and terminal boundary condition V(x,T)=g(x). The infinite-horizon and finite-horizon settings are mixed throughout without reconciliation, and the proofs in A.1/A.2 are heuristic Taylor expansions (with an unjustified split of max over two horizon segments) rather than rigorous viscosity-solution arguments.

Theorem 3.4 is essentially trivial and largely disconnected from the method: it analyzes a linear fixed-point iteration ζ(k+1)=G(ζ(k)) whose contraction property reduces to requiring Lf·Δt < 1 — an assumption, not a result. Moreover, the method never actually runs this iteration; it uses a single one-step VGI target, so the 'convergence' theorem provides no meaningful guarantee for the trained system.

Lemma 3.3 (policy improvement) is not credible as stated: the actor update is a stochastic policy-gradient step on Eq. (9) (advantage-weighted log-likelihood), not the argmax operation assumed in the proof; the proof in A.3 is hand-wavy, conflates one-step and trajectory returns, ignores non-stationarity from simultaneous agent updates, and the 'sufficiently small step size' condition is never formalized. No convergence or improvement guarantee for the actual algorithm is provided.

There is a fundamental tension in the method's use of models: the HJB residual uses the true f and r, while the VGI target relies on gradients of learned models ∇xrϕ and ∇xfψ. The method is therefore heavily model-based, but the consequences of model error on the HJB residual and advantage estimates are not analyzed or ablated; the residual at Eq. (4) evaluated with what control u (current policy vs. maximizing u*) is also left ambiguous.

Baselines are weak and incomplete for the central claim. Only two MPE and a handful of MuJoCo tasks are used, with three adapted CT baselines; no comparison against strong discrete-time MARL methods (MAPPO, FACMAC, MADDPG on the main benchmarks) is provided, so the claim of 'consistently outperforming existing baselines' and superiority over DTRL rests largely on one didactic MADDPG comparison. Also, the CT baselines (DPI, IPI, CT-MBRL) were designed for single-agent settings, and details of their multi-agent adaptation/fair tuning are absent.

Statistical rigor is thin: five random seeds with no significance testing or quantitative tables (only noisy learning-curve plots); results in several MuJoCo tasks (e.g., Swimmer, Walker) show overlapping confidence bands, weakening the 'consistently outperforms' claim. In Fig. 3, the w/o-VGI value contour operates on a wildly different scale (≈0.81–0.86 vs. ground truth ≈0.18–0.24), which is unexplained and suggests a possible normalization or training pathology that is not discussed.

Key methodological details are missing: the critical loss weights λterm, λanchor, λg in Eq. (18) are never specified (the hyperparameter table omits them), despite the paper's own ablation showing results are highly sensitive to these weights. The paper also states five seeds while Table 1 lists seeds 111–120 (ten values).

Credit assignment in the cooperative setting is unaddressed: the actor loss uses the advantage of the joint action for each decentralized agent's update, ignoring the standard CTDE counterfactual/credit-assignment machinery; it is unclear whether gains come from the CT formulation or simply from the centralized critic with model-based bootstrapping.

Presentation and scholarship issues further erode confidence: the method is called CT-MARL in the abstract/intro but VIP later (and 'VPI' in Fig. 9), duplicate references ([8]=[9], [24]=[25]), typos ('chllenges', 'outperforms'), and the claim that PINN+RL for CT-MARL is 'unexplored' overstates novelty given cited HJB-PINN + PPO work [27] and value-gradient PINN literature [50, 51], from which the VGI idea draws heavily.
No code release is mentioned, and given the sensitivity to loss weighting, model training, and Δt sampling, reproducibility without the code appears difficult.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: continuous-time MARL via HJB/PINNs, with a clear motivation (curse of dimensionality, non-stationarity, value-gradient fidelity).

The VGI module is a sensible and relatively novel idea: bootstrapping value-gradient targets along trajectories via the dynamics Jacobian, serving as a surrogate for supervised gradient learning when ground-truth gradients are unavailable.

Good empirical design: continuous-time variants of MPE and multi-agent MuJoCo, a didactic coupled-oscillator task with exact LQR ground truth that enables direct validation of both V and ∇xV (Fig. 3, Fig. 9).
Reasonable ablation coverage: VGI removal, activation function choice (Tanh vs. ReLU), loss-term weighting, per-term ablations (Fig. 6), and time-interval robustness comparison against MADDPG.
Hyperparameters, architectures, and environment modifications are documented, supporting moderate reproducibility.
weaknesses: Technical soundness issues in the theory. Theorem 3.4's contraction claim is flawed: β = e^{-ρ∆t}(1 + Lf∆t) < 1 does not follow from ∆t being small; as ∆t → 0, β → 1 + (Lf − ρ)∆t, so contraction requires Lf < ρ, an unstated and generally unrealistic assumption. The convergence result is also trivially per-state (one-step affine map) and says little about joint training.

Lemma 3.3 (policy improvement) is essentially unproven: the appendix proof analyzes an argmax policy improvement, not the actual algorithm (one gradient step on Lp under a stochastic policy), and the derivation is sloppy (index confusion, informal claims about 'sufficiently small step size' guaranteeing Q^{new} ≥ Q^{old}).

Inconsistent formulation: Eq. (2) defines V over an infinite horizon while Lemma 3.1 imposes a finite-horizon terminal condition V(x,T) = g(x); the derivation in A.1 conflates the two, and the proof mixes max over u with the actor-network parameterization without reconciling when the actor is not optimal.

The VGI target relies on learned dynamics and reward models (fψ, rϕ), so ∇x r and ∇x f inherit model bias and compounding error; the paper does not analyze or empirically isolate how model error affects gradient fidelity, which is central to the claimed contribution.

Baseline coverage is weak for a MARL paper: only three continuous-time baselines (CT-MBRL, DPI, IPI) plus the internal ablation. Missing comparisons to strong modern discrete-time MARL methods (MAPPO, QMIX, FACMAC — the latter is only cited), to HJB-PPO [27] which is the closest related method, and no explanation of the model-based-vs-model-free fairness of comparisons.
Claims of 'consistently outperforms' rest on 5-seed mean curves without statistical significance testing; some ablations (Fig. 6) are shown for only one environment.

Limited novelty beyond combination: PINNs for HJB [27, 34, 51], value-gradient learning, and model-based actor-critic are all established; the contribution is primarily an adaptation to the cooperative CT-MARL setting, and the paper itself concedes competitive/mixed settings are out of scope.

Notable polish problems that undermine confidence: duplicated references ([8]/[9], [24]/[25]), garbled citation [30], inconsistent naming (VGI vs. 'VIP module', 'VPI' in Fig. 9), typos ('chllenges'), and Section 4 referring to the method as 'Value Iteration via PINN' while the rest calls it CT-MARL/VIP.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely underexplored area: continuous-time MARL via HJB-based value learning, where prior CTRL work is almost exclusively single-agent; this is a relevant and timely problem.

The proposed VIP framework is clearly described, including the critic losses (HJB residual, anchor, VGI), the advantage-based decentralized actor updates, and a full training algorithm with architecture and hyperparameter details in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.

The evaluation is reasonably broad: continuous-time variants of MPE and multi-agent MuJoCo (up to ~113 state dimensions), a didactic LQR benchmark with exact ground-truth value and gradients for quantitative validation, comparisons against four CT-RL baselines plus three discrete-time MARL baselines, ablations (VGI, loss weighting, activation functions), robustness to noise, and sensitivity to the discretization step.
The paper is honest about its scope (deterministic dynamics, cooperative settings) and shows the expected degradation under stochasticity rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Theoretical soundness gaps. Lemma 3.3 (policy improvement) is not rigorously proven: the appendix proof assumes an argmax-style policy improvement step that does not match the actual stochastic-policy-gradient update in Eq. 8, invokes an unclear assumption ('goal state function stays invariant'), and never connects to the 'sufficiently small step size' claim. Theorem 3.4 is essentially trivial: contraction follows directly from a first-order Euler expansion requiring Lf*Δt → 0, and the frozen time-invariant map analysis says little about the joint, nonstationary training process.

Internal tension in the critic objective. The residual Aθ = -ρVθ + ∇Vθ·f + r is simultaneously (a) minimized towards zero via Lres for actions sampled from the current (suboptimal) policy and (b) used as the policy-improvement signal. If the residual loss succeeds, the advantage signal vanishes; if not, the critic is biased. This well-known subtlety of HJB-residual actor-critic schemes is not analyzed or even acknowledged, and the distinction from the correct Hamiltonian maximization (u* = argmax H) is blurred.

Limited technical novelty. The method is largely a combination of existing ingredients: HJB-PINN critics (HJBPPO, Shilova et al., Meng et al.), continuous-time policy iteration (Lee & Sutton), and value-gradient learning/propagation ideas; applying them to cooperative MARL is the main contribution, and the VGI estimator is a one-step unrolling that follows directly from the dynamic programming principle.

The method is model-based (learned dynamics and reward models) but there is no analysis or experiment isolating the effect of model error on the HJB residual and VGI targets, which is a significant confounder for the claimed value-accuracy gains.

Evaluation concerns: only 5 seeds with no statistical significance testing; several learning curves show overlapping confidence regions (e.g., Swimmer, Ant tasks); the discount factor (ρ=0.95) and fixed episode length (50) sit uneasily with the infinite-horizon formulation; baseline CT methods (DPI, IPI) may be disadvantaged by adaptation choices without sensitivity analysis.

Presentation and consistency issues: naming inconsistencies (VIP vs. VPI in Fig. 10), typos ('didactic case', 'pretty unstable', proof 'is posted at'), incomplete citation for Mukherjee & Liu (no venue/year), and duplicate references (Lowe et al. 2017a/b).

The claimed scalability ('scales to complex cooperative multi-agent dynamics') is only weakly supported; results at the highest-dimensional tasks (e.g., Ant variants) show modest or noisy gains over baselines, and the tension between PINN training cost and the CoD motivation is not quantified (no runtime/compute comparisons).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: continuous-time MARL via HJB-based value learning, which is a meaningful gap relative to the largely single-agent CTRL literature.
The proposed framework is clearly described, with a coherent CTDE actor-critic structure, a PINN critic with HJB residuals, and a value-gradient consistency (VGI) loss that is intuitively motivated.

Evaluation coverage is broad: continuous-time variants of MPE and multi-agent MuJoCo across eight settings (up to 6 agents / 113 state dimensions), four continuous-time baselines, three discrete-time baselines, ablations on VGI/loss terms/activation functions, plus a didactic coupled-oscillator task with analytical LQR ground truth for value and gradient verification.
The didactic benchmark with exact value/gradient ground truth is a nice touch and effectively illustrates the value-gradient accuracy claims (Figs. 3 and 10).
weaknesses: Theory is weak and partly flawed. Lemma 3.3 (policy improvement) proof is informal and appears incorrect: it inconsistently mixes per-step discounts (e−ρδt vs e−ρt1), assumes 'the goal state function stays invariant,' and does not handle stochastic policies, constrained action sets, or the multi-agent setting where other agents simultaneously update. The claim Q^πnew ≥ Q^πold for a single gradient step on the actor loss is asserted rather than established.

Theorem 3.4 is trivial: G(ζ) = b + Aζ is an affine map whose contraction is a one-line observation, and its 'unique fixed point' depends on (xt, ut) and on the currently learned (imperfect) dynamics/reward models; no analysis of how model errors propagate into the VGI target is provided, despite models being trained jointly with the critic.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence. Figure 8 claims VIP 'maintains a nearly constant return across different time intervals,' yet Appendix C.4/Fig. 13 shows VIP's return degrading sharply from roughly −9 to −30 as Δt grows to 0.2 in the same environment. The paper states five random seeds, but Table 1 lists seeds 111–120 (ten seeds). Eq. 17 is described as combining 'all four losses' but contains only three. Appendix Figure 10 caption says 'VPI' instead of 'VIP.' A 'code is available at this link' placeholder appears without an actual link.

Novelty is limited. The method is largely a combination of known ingredients: HJB-residual PINN critics (e.g., HJBPPO, Shilova et al.), a TD anchor loss, and a value-gradient consistency term that closely resembles classical value-gradient learning (e.g., Fairbank & Alonso's VGDL and related differential-RL literature), which is not cited or compared. The main novelty is assembling these in a MARL setting rather than a new algorithmic or theoretical contribution.

The critic loss only enforces the HJB residual with the current (non-optimal) policy's actions, so the quantity Aθ used as the policy 'advantage' equals the HJB residual, not a true advantage; the gap between optimizing this surrogate and improving the actual return under a jointly learned policy is not analyzed, and non-stationarity from simultaneous agent updates is ignored in the improvement argument.

Evaluation lacks rigor: no final-performance tables with standard deviations, no statistical significance tests, and several baseline curves collapse (e.g., DPI, IPI), making relative comparisons hard to interpret. The method is restricted to deterministic dynamics; the stochastic-robustness experiment in Appendix C.3 shows substantial degradation, and the high-dimensional claims (113-dim states) are not validated against value-approximation error at scale.
Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code link, and several key details (how the VGI target's Δt is chosen during training, λanchor/λg values, per-environment differences) are underspecified.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and relevant problem: continuous-time (HJB-based) RL in multi-agent cooperative settings, where most prior CTRL work is single-agent. The positioning and related work coverage are solid.

The proposed framework is reasonably complete: HJB-residual PINN critic, a value-gradient iteration (VGI) auxiliary loss, TD-style anchor loss, and a continuous-time advantage used for decentralized actor updates, all tied together with a clear algorithm (Algorithm 1) and released code.

A fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation: continuous-time variants of MPE and multi-agent MuJoCo (up to 6 agents / 113 state dims), multiple CT baselines (ODE/DPI/IPI/HJBPPO), DT baselines (MADDPG/MAPPO/MATD3), 5 seeds, and several ablations (VGI removal, loss-term weighting, activation function choice, Δt sensitivity, noise robustness).
The didactic LQR coupled-oscillator study is a nice touch: it permits ground-truth value and gradient comparisons, making the VGI contribution interpretable (Figs. 3, 10).
Time-discretization robustness experiments (Figs. 8, 13) directly support the core motivation that CT methods are more invariant to decision-interval changes than DT methods.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty. The VGI estimator (Eq. 10) is essentially a one-step semi-discretization of the Bellman equation applied in gradient space; closely related ideas exist in value-gradient learning and HJB-PINN literature (e.g., Zhang et al. 2024b, Meng et al. 2024, Nakamura-Zimmerer et al. 2021), which the paper acknowledges but does not clearly differentiate from.

The theoretical results are weak. Theorem 3.4 is a trivial Banach fixed-point argument on an affine map whose contraction requires 'Δt sufficiently small' — an assumption asserted rather than characterized. The proof of Lemma 3.3 (policy improvement) is informal and internally inconsistent (mixing e^{-ρδt} and e^{-ρt_k} factors, silently swapping expectations and policies, and never actually using the 'sufficiently small step size' premise), so a central claim of the actor update is not rigorously supported.

A tension undermines the headline claim of 'continuous-time' learning: the VGI target and anchor loss require a learned dynamics model fψ trained as a discrete-time next-state predictor, with the continuous-time derivative recovered by finite differences (Eq. 13). This reintroduces exactly the discretization and step-size sensitivity the paper criticizes, as confirmed by the sharp performance degradation for Δt ≳ 0.15 (Fig. 13). The method is thus closer to semi-discretized model-based RL than a genuinely discretization-free CT method.

The anchor loss (Eq. 16) is a standard TD bootstrap; combined with the finite-difference dynamics model, it is unclear how much of the performance comes from VGI versus the anchor term, especially since Fig. 4 shows VIP and VIP w/o VGI curves largely overlapping in some MPE tasks.

Baseline fairness concerns: the CT baselines (DPI, IPI, ODE, HJBPPO) are single-agent methods adapted to MARL, with adaptation details (e.g., 'we discretize the integral... and fit a policy') underspecified. The DT baselines are evaluated under randomly sampled integration intervals, a setting designed to break them; a fairer comparison (DT methods with action repetition or matched intervals) is missing.

Evidence of advantage is mixed in places: several learning curves (Figs. 2, 4, 9) show overlapping confidence bands and modest final-return differences, and MPE results are close to baselines; the claim of 'consistently outperforming' is stronger than the plots support.

Scope limitations are significant: deterministic dynamics only (stochastic settings degrade sharply, App. C.3), cooperative settings only, and dependence on bounded-Jacobian/small-Δt conditions. The paper's claims of scalability are also only indirectly supported — no wall-clock/compute comparison showing PINN critics are practical at 113 dimensions.

Presentation issues: inconsistent naming (CT-MARL vs. VIP vs. 'VPI' in Fig. 10 caption), several typos and informal phrasing ('pretty unstable', 'didactic case'), and Eq. 17 says 'all four losses' while only three terms appear.

Hyperparameters (discount ρ=0.95, replay buffer, soft-update rate) appear borrowed from discrete-time practice, and there is no sensitivity analysis for λ_anchor, λ_g beyond three coarse weight configurations.
